newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Tin organisation seeks for reason to go on.
newsitem.headline: Tin organisation seeks for reason to go on.

text.p: The Association of Tin Producing Countries (ATPC) is groping to find a reason for its existence with its export quota system in tatters and membership falling, traders and officials said on Wednesday.

"They have to find a reason to exist. The ATPC is now a dog without any teeth since its quota system is impossible to meet anyway and nobody follows it," a tin trader in Singapore told Reuters. "They have to reassess their relevance."

Tin mining officials attending the September 23-24 ATPC ministerial conference in Singapore said the association's supply rationalisation scheme (SRS) had failed because only a few members were willing to stick by their quotas.
"The SRS is not adhered to at all. Both producers and consumers have basically ignored the scheme," said an official at a major tin company. "Nobody has taken it seriously."
"Malaysia and Indonesia don't give a damn about those quotas," said a Singapore-based tin trader. "They (the ATPC) leave it open for anybody to violate."
Tin company officials in Malaysia said any attempt to revive the SRS was seen as futile. The ATPC said tin exports by its members in 1995 reached 100,023 tonnes, 10 percent above quotas for the year.

"It will not work," said one official with another tin company. "The SRS was introduced to stabilise tin prices after the collapse of the International Tin Council (in 1985). To me, it had no impact at all."
He said some ATPC members had over-produced while others, like Malaysia, could not meet their quotas.
Kuntoro Mangkusubroto, director-general of mining at the Mines and Energy Ministry in Indonesia, said last month the SRS was dead.
"We want a free market for tin because it is very effective for us," he said.
Another problem plaguing the group is falling membership, analysts said.
The ATPC links Australia, Bolivia, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand and Zaire. Brazil is an observer.
But Thailand said it would pull out of the group by the end of this month because it was now a net importer of tin. Zaire, which now produces almost no tin, has skipped the last few meetings.
Brazil, which indicated last year it would join the organisation, has baulked and said it would just maintain its observer status because it finds the ATPC too weak.
"Our entrance now would be useless," Giovanni Toniatti, secretary of Mines and Metalurgy at the Mines and Energy Ministry, said in an interview on Tuesday.
In the United States, tin traders were even blunter.
"The ATPC is a dead old duck. It's history," a tin trading and producer executive said. The group's money would be better spent on the International Tin Research Institute, he said.
"Whatever they do is a non-event. If they disbanded, it means nothing," another U.S. tin trader added.
The United States is the world's biggest consumer of tin, importing 33,200 tons of the 45,000 tons it used in 1995.
